summary:
The main idea behind Lychee Juicebox was to make a data sonification experience that was customizable and intuitive. It is made for data represented on world maps

Pick one of the maps on the site, or upload your own world map. Then choose a place on the globe and decide how much of the surrounding area to hear. The app scans the colors and brightness in that part of the image and turns them into a short piece of sound. You can choose how the scan moves and pick a sound style and length.

As your mix plays, a scan-line follows the scan and small color bars show what the app is reading. You can listen in normal, 3D, or 8D mode; headphones make the movement easier to hear. DJ mode lets you drag through the sound yourself, while an optional instrument mode plays it back in the browser.

The result is an artistic take on the image you chose. It isn’t a recording of Earth or a direct translation of the scientific measurements behind a map. We wanted to make Earth imagery something you could explore with your ears, experiment with, and share.
details:
Principle:

The program is made up of 2 main parts: the Next.js frontend and Python FastAPI backend. The backend turns the image file into a .wav file using OpenCV and STRAUSS. The frontend handles location, map cropping and other options selected by the user; sends the cropped image to the backend and receives a .wav file to display it to the user. It is important to note that the sound generated comes from an image file and not from raw physical data.

FastAPI:

FastAPI connects the Next.js frontend to the Python sonification system. It receives the cropped image and selected settings, validates them, passes the image to OpenCV for analysis and STRAUSS for sound synthesis, then returns the generated WAV file and color-analysis data to the frontend. It also provides sound-template information, API documentation, request limits, error handling, and CORS support.

Backend:

The backend checks and accepts still PNG, JPEG, WebP, BMP, and TIFF images, subject to its size and 8-bit limits; the website upload control accepts PNG and JPEG raster maps. If it is within criteria, OpenCV decodes the pixels of the image and the backend converts images into RGB values between 0 and 1.

The backend samples the selected image at 48 positions, with 12 pitch bands at each position. This means 12 pitch levels are present in all scan positions. Left-to-right scans use 48 image columns and 12 vertical bands. Clockwise scans use 48 rays, 7.5 degrees apart, with bands running from the center to the edge; pitches are higher near the center. Center-outward and outside-inward scans sample expanding or contracting rings, with pitch bands arranged as angular sectors around each ring.

Each of the red, blue, green colors are given their own “voice”, which is basically what kind of sound they will produce. For example, red might produce a clicking sound, blue may produce a howling sound and green may produce a watery sound. (Keep in mind these are not actual sound options and only examples)

Then, the backend converts RGB color values into mapped HSV values. Hue determines the blend of voices. Red is anchored at 0, green is anchored at 120, blue is anchored at 240 degrees. Anything in between contributes to both neighboring hues. So yellow will contribute to the voice of both red and green.

Saturation determines how much of the sound is made up of the colored voices versus a neutral grey voice. Colors of high saturation will produce less grey sound and more red, blue or green sound. The grey sound effectively acts as another “voice” in this context, appearing more as saturation goes down.

The sounds produced by each color is determined by the sound template, discussed in the Frontend section.

The brightness is calculated using a weighted combination of the red, green and blue values. Each voice's relative volume is proportional to the brightness. For example, dark green will produce a quieter sound than light green (in the same recording)

The band determines the pitch of the sound. For example in Left-to-Right scanning, a band of lower latitude will produce a sound with lower pitch than a band of higher latitude. In clockwise scans, bands run from center to edge so pitch gets higher as the band gets closer to the center.

STRAUSS uses HSV values as written above to synthesize sound before the backend returns a .wav file. Spatialization and normalisation are optional.

Frontend:

The algorithm itself can be used to turn any supported image file into a .wav file. The website allows many other features that allow the user to fine tune their sonification experience.

Firstly, there is a tutorial video at the top of the website presenting all of the features visually, aiming to improve User Experience. There is also a website tour that can be accessed at the bottom of the page.

The features presented by the website include:

-Location Selection

Instead of listening to data from all around the world, people may want to sonify only data from a region. For example, only generating sound files from their country may be preferable. To implement this, a location selection system was put into use.The user can select a location from the world map. According to the location selected, the program can generate a .wav file using only a variable radius around that location. However, this is not the end of the capabilities of the program. There are several selection shapes, consisting of circle selection, square selection and full map selection. On top of that, advanced location settings allow for specific cities or coordinates to be entered into the system instead of a rough selection on the globe.

-Map Selection

The website offers many still and animated visual maps downloaded from the NASA Earth Information Center (EIC) database (identified clearly in the sources section) and an “Actual World Map” from Three.js, from which users can choose. On top of the maps pre-loaded onto the website, the users can input their own maps as jpeg or png with supported dimensions. (It will treat the uploaded image as a full world map so any other type of image will not have meaningful coordinates.) The location selected on the world map is found on the inputted or selected world map. The sound is generated from the area around the location. The size of this area is variable and can be changed by the user.

-Scan path

The scan path, explained briefly in the Backend section, determines how the algorithm will break the cropped image file from frontend into parts that can be processed as sound. Put simply, it determines how the area will be scanned. There are 4 modes total:

Left-to-Right: Scans the cropped image from left to right.

Clockwise: Scans the image as a radius around a centre point, recommended specifically for circle selection.

Center outward: Scans the area as a circle that slowly grows from the center of the selected area.

Outside inward: Scans the area as a circle that slowly shrinks from the outer part of the selected area.

-Sound templates

Other than the original sounds of the red, green and blue colors; other sound templates have been prepared. For example, the “Heavenly” template uses different sounds than the “Medieval” template. We highly recommend trying out different templates.

Also, after sound is generated, the frontend can detect notes from the generated audio to resynthesize an interpretation of the sound using one instrument from Tone.js. The instrument styles include soft keys, glass bells or string pad. Only one instrument can play at a time.

-3D and 8D sound capability:

One of the defining features of Lychee Juicebox is its compatibility with 3D and 8D sound technologies. If selected, 3D sound allows for spatial stereo sound, which gives the effect of sound moving as scan line moves on the screen.

8D sound carries this effect to the next level, adding moving left-right panning and short cross-ear delays. This amplifies the effect by offering a wider, moving headphone effect that immerses the user in the sound even more.

3D and 8D sound are best experienced using headphones. In this manner, it is almost as if the sound is coming from the user's environment itself. However, the effect is definitely noticeable from laptop or cellphone speakers.

We highly recommend trying 3D and 8D sound modes as it is much better being experienced one on one.

(Please keep in mind the term 8D sound isn’t used in its traditional internet context but in the context of an improved 3D sound mode offered by our website)

-Length Selection

The length of the audio file to be produced is determined here. 10, 20 or 30 seconds can be chosen.

-Color and Brightness Tracking

After the settings are set and the backend creates a sound file from the selected map and region; the bars show the relative contributions of the four sound voices at the current scan position. The window also shows brightness. This so users know exactly where the sound they’re hearing is coming from.

-Dynamic Playing on Map

The region selected is shown on the screen. While playing the sound generated from the region, the scan line used to produce the sound can be seen dynamically moving on the region selected on the world map according to its scan path.

-DJ Mode

The scan line shown on the region under Dynamic Playing can be controlled by mouse or touchscreen input to control the timestamp. DJ Mode needs to be toggled on to access this feature.

-Mobile Compatibility

The website is fully adapted for mobile use.

-Accessibility Features

(Accessibility features have their own tab from which they can be accessed.)

>Larger texts for increased readability.

>High Contrast mode for less eye strain

>Reduced Motion mode

>Screen reader guidance, keyboard navigation, and browser text-to-speech feedback for better experience for blind or partially-blind users

Tools used:

-Python

-HTML

-Next.js

-JavaScript

-TypeScript

-CSS

-STRAUSS

-Tone.js

-FastAPI

-NASA Earth Information Center (EIC) Resources

-OpenCV

-Vercel

Creativity:

Brainstorming was one of the most essential parts of our project. We spent a lot of time figuring out what could make our Earth Information Jukebox feel different. This required a massive amount of time spent just thinking about what we can create.

One of our most creative ideas was adding Normal, 3D (spatial audio) and even 8D options for the user. This improved the experience of the user as we let them choose what kind of audio they want.

Another idea was adding “DJ Mode”. To the frontend of our product, we added a brand new feature called DJ Mode, which lets the user adjust the scan position. We also have a color and brightness tracker right underneath. This shows which colors are dominant at that position (red, blue, green or gray/neutral) while also displaying a brightness percentage.

Intended Impact:

Our main goal is to make Earth imagery easier to explore by giving people a way to hear its patterns. Users can pick a place on the globe, choose a map, and listen to how the sound changes as they move across it. We hope this makes Earth science more approachable and sparks curiosity in people who might never have thought to explore a NASA map. By combining maps with sound, we hope to reach people who are new to Earth science and give people who find visual maps difficult to read another way to explore them.

Factors Considered:

User Experience:

UI was a very important criteria on our side. We needed to make sure the project is simple to use and easy to understand. Therefore we considered how easy the jukebox would be to use, how clearly the sound would reflect the map, and how people might prefer to listen.

Additional Features:

In DJ Mode, we added a scan positioner so that users could freely explore which color was dominant at which position, and also adjust the scanner by holding it or playing with the slider . We also offered three listening modes so users could choose how much movement they wanted to hear.

Clear sound mapping:

How would users know why an instrument got louder or why a note changed? The color and brightness tracker helps them make that connection. We added it so users could connect changes in sound to the part of the map they were exploring
